Pelorus Voyages offers a companion discount for qualifying passengers travelling together on the same itinerary. The companion discount is 15 percent off the lower-priced passenger's voyage package. The discount applies to the base voyage package only; add-ons, excursions, and the Extraction Coverage insurance add-on are not discounted under the companion benefit.

To qualify for the companion discount, both passengers must hold Pathfinder loyalty tier status at the time of booking. The tier check is performed at the time the companion discount is requested; if either passenger is not yet Pathfinder tier, the discount is not available for that booking. A discount applied at booking is not reversed if either passenger's tier changes subsequently; conversely, if a passenger achieves Pathfinder tier after booking, the companion discount cannot be applied retroactively.

Both passengers must also be on the same itinerary and the same departure date. The companion discount is not available for passengers on different itineraries or different departure windows even if they are travelling as companions in some sense. The discount is applied to the lower-priced passenger's fare; if both passengers have the same cabin class, the system applies the discount to the second booking processed.

To apply the companion discount, both passengers must have linked Pelorus Voyages accounts. Account linking is done through the account portal by sending a companion link request to the other passenger's registered email address.

Once the link is accepted, the discount appears as an option during checkout when both passengers are booking the same itinerary and departure window.

The companion discount cannot be combined with group booking rates, corporate account discounts, or promotional codes unless the promotion's terms explicitly state otherwise. In most cases the companion discount is more favourable than a standard group rate for two passengers; the booking system will show the best available rate and the applicable conditions.

Companions do not need to share a cabin to access the companion discount. Two Pathfinder tier passengers who prefer separate Pathfinder suites can each receive the discount as long as both are on the same itinerary and departure date.

Corporate accounts are available to organisations that book five or more Pelorus Voyages voyages per calendar year across their employees or clients. Corporate accounts offer consolidated billing, dedicated account management, and access to group itinerary scheduling for large bookings. To establish a corporate account, contact the Pelorus Voyages corporate travel team directly; a corporate account cannot be established through the standard online booking portal.

Corporate account holders are invoiced monthly for all bookings made in the preceding month, on net-30 payment terms from invoice issue. Payment is by bank transfer only; credit and debit cards are not accepted for corporate account billing. Late payment incurs a 1.5 percent monthly finance charge on the outstanding balance.

Corporate account administrators can view all active bookings, make changes, and initiate cancellations on behalf of employees through the corporate portal. Individual employees cannot cancel their own bookings under a corporate account without administrator authorisation.

Corporate accounts interact with the Orbital Points loyalty programme in a specific way. Points earned on corporate-account bookings are by default credited to the Pelorus Voyages corporate pool, not to the individual passenger's personal loyalty account. Corporate account administrators can choose to direct Points to individual passengers instead; this setting is configured per booking at the time of booking, not retroactively.

Passengers who travel on a personal booking not through the corporate account earn Points to their personal account normally, regardless of their employer's corporate account status.

The companion discount is not available for bookings made through a corporate account. Group rates and corporate account pricing are separate discount structures that do not stack; Pelorus Voyages will apply whichever discount is more favourable to the booking at the time of checkout.

Corporate clients booking dedicated vessel charters or custom itineraries should discuss requirements with the corporate travel team well in advance of desired travel dates. Custom itineraries are subject to fleet availability and require a minimum notice period of 18 months.

Pelorus Voyages accepts the following payment methods for all voyage bookings, add-on purchases, and excursion fees. Not all methods are available for all transaction types; restrictions are noted below.

Major credit and debit cards are accepted for all transaction types including deposits, balance payments, add-ons, and on-voyage purchases at the bar and excursion desks. Accepted card networks are Visa, Mastercard, and American Express. Cards issued by non-Earth banking institutions must be registered in the account portal before use; some Mars Colonial Bank and Lunar Credit Union cards require a one-time identity verification step on first use.

Bank transfer is accepted for voyage deposits and balance payments only. Bank transfers are not accepted for on-voyage purchases. Pelorus Voyages supports SWIFT, IBAN, and the Interplanetary Clearing Network (ICN) for non-Earth accounts.

Orbital Credits are the Pelorus Voyages stored-value account. Credits can be loaded by credit card, bank transfer, or as a refund from a cancelled voyage. Orbital Credits are accepted for all transaction types including on-voyage purchases and can be used to pay any portion of a booking. Credits expire 24 months after the last transaction on the account if no qualifying voyage has taken place. Orbital Points may be redeemed toward voyage bookings and cabin class upgrades through the points redemption function in the account portal. Points redemption converts a points allocation into a voyage credit that offsets the payment amount. Points redemption for upgrades must be completed at least seven days before departure; within seven days, upgrades must be paid by cash or card.

No minimum age is waivable. Age limits marked as firm cannot be overridden by parental consent, signed waiver, or any other mechanism. Passengers who present at an excursion with a minor below the firm minimum age will be turned away; the excursion fee will not be refunded unless the age restriction was clearly misrepresented in the booking system (contact support if you believe this occurred).

Photography is welcome and encouraged at all Pelorus Voyages destinations. Most stops have no restrictions beyond common courtesy. The exceptions are the heritage protection sites, where specific rules apply and violations carry formal consequences.

At Tranquility Base Heritage Site, the following photography rules apply under the Outer Space Heritage Preservation Act of 2041 and the Lunar Heritage Authority access agreement. Photography from the marked perimeter is permitted without restriction and is the primary activity for most visitors. Flash photography is prohibited within 50 metres of the heritage boundary flagging. Drone or remotely piloted aircraft of any kind are prohibited within the entire heritage zone, which extends 2 kilometres beyond the visible perimeter. Laser pointers or laser range-finding equipment may not be directed at the flag, the Lunar Module descent stage, or any other heritage object.

hich extends 2 kilometres beyond the visible perimeter. Laser pointers or laser range-finding equipment may not be directed at the flag, the Lunar Module descent stage, or any other heritage object.

At the Fra Mauro zone (Lunar Golf Links area), the same drone prohibition applies within 500 metres of the Shepard Shot Marker. Approach within 20 metres of the Shepard Shot Marker is prohibited; photography is permitted from beyond that distance.

At the Cydonia Formation complex on Mars, photography is permitted from designated viewing areas. Drone use within the Cydonia Category B scientific preservation zone is prohibited without a research permit issued by the Mars Surface Heritage Authority. Personal drones above 500 grams are prohibited entirely in the preservation zone; sub-500-gram recreational drones require advance notification to the Cydonia site coordinator.

e Heritage Authority. Personal drones above 500 grams are prohibited entirely in the preservation zone; sub-500-gram recreational drones require advance notification to the Cydonia site coordinator.

Consequences for violations are significant. A violation of photography or drone rules at Tranquility Base or Fra Mauro is reported immediately to the Lunar Heritage Authority by the tour guide. Consequences range from permanent exclusion from heritage sites to criminal prosecution under the OSHPA 2041, which carries fines and in serious cases custodial sentences. Pelorus Voyages is legally required to report violations and does not have discretion to decline reporting.

## Equipment rental credits

A rental credit entitles the passenger to one rental of any single equipment item at any stop where rental is available. Standard rental items include: cold-suit gear (Titan only — though cold suits are mandatory and provided, a rental credit can offset the standard excursion surcharge), EVA equipment upgrades, photography equipment, golf club sets at the Lunar Golf Links, and Ceres surface sports equipment. Rental credits are redeemed at the excursion check-in desk at each stop. Unused credits do not carry over to future voyages.

Personal golf clubs declared and cleared at Moon Base 7 are transported to the Fra Mauro excursion site at no additional charge and count against the passenger's personal mass allowance. A standard six-club set with bag weighs approximately 4.5 kg.

## Prohibited from mass allowance exemptions

All of the following count toward personal mass allowance with no exemption: medical equipment (CPAP machines, portable oxygen, injectable medications with cooling cases), camera bodies and lenses, personal golf clubs, and clothing. ## Baggage measurement

Baggage is measured at the Earth launch terminal only. Individual stops do not re-weigh passengers' belongings. Overweight baggage fees assessed at Earth launch apply to the full voyage and are charged before boarding.

Prescription and over-the-counter medications for personal use are not counted against the passenger's personal mass allowance. Medications carried in original pharmacy containers and supported by a current prescription or physician letter travel exempt from the weight limit. This exemption applies to the medications themselves; the case, cooling unit, or bag used to carry them counts toward the mass allowance.

Medications that require temperature-controlled storage — including certain biologics, insulin, and some liquid antibiotics — may be transported in a personal insulated medication case. The case contents (the medications) are mass-exempt; the case itself counts toward the allowance. Pelorus Voyages recommends cases that weigh no more than 1 kilogram when empty; the medical bay on the vessel can provide supplementary temperature-controlled storage for medications on a pre-arranged basis for passengers whose requirements exceed what a personal case provides.

the medical bay on the vessel can provide supplementary temperature-controlled storage for medications on a pre-arranged basis for passengers whose requirements exceed what a personal case provides. Contact accessibility support before departure to arrange this.

All medications must be declared on the passenger's medical section in the account portal before departure. The declaration does not need to include dosing details but should list each medication by name (brand and generic if known), the condition it treats, and whether it requires refrigeration or special storage. This information is provided to the vessel's flight surgeon before departure and is used to ensure the medical bay inventory is compatible with the passenger's treatment plan.

Requirements vary by waypoint authority; the Moon Base 7 and Ceres Waystation customs desks publish current controlled substance declaration requirements on their respective official information portals. Pelorus Voyages cannot advise on the specific requirements of third-party waypoint authorities; passengers with controlled substance prescriptions should research applicable requirements well before departure.

The following items may not be brought aboard any Pelorus Voyages vessel or taken onto any surface excursion, regardless of cabin class. This list applies in addition to all standard international spaceflight safety regulations. Violations discovered at baggage screening result in confiscation; violations discovered aboard the vessel during flight may result in immediate disembarkation at the next stop at the passenger's expense.

Combustible and flammable materials are prohibited. This includes liquid-fuel lighters, strike-anywhere matches, aerosol cans with flammable propellants, and camping fuel canisters of any type. Battery-powered lighters with an enclosed heating element are permitted.

Unsealed biological samples are prohibited. This applies both to biological material brought from Earth and to any biological or geological material collected at a destination.

## 1. Standard Cancellation Policy

Pelorus Voyages provides a free cancellation window of 14 days from the date of booking for all itineraries and cabin classes. Cancellations submitted within 14 days of booking receive a full refund of any amounts paid, with no administrative fee.

After the 14-day free window closes, cancellation fees apply based on how far in advance of the departure date the cancellation is submitted:

- **More than 30 days before departure** — 25 percent fee; 75 percent refunded
- **7 to 29 days before departure** — 50 percent fee; 50 percent refunded
- **48 hours to 6 days before departure** — 75 percent fee; 25 percent refunded
- **Within 48 hours of departure window** — non-refundable; full voyage price is forfeited

These fees are calculated on the total voyage package price per passenger.

The fee schedule applies to the base voyage and cabin class; excursion add-ons purchased separately are subject to their own cancellation terms (see the upgrade and add-on policy in the Passenger Handbook for the 48-hour add-on cutoff).

Cancellations must be submitted in writing through the Pelorus Voyages account portal or by contacting bookings support directly. Cancellation is effective from the date and time the written request is received and logged, not from the date the passenger decided to cancel. Verbal cancellations are not accepted.

## 2. Group Booking Cancellations

Groups of eight or more passengers travelling under a single group booking reference are subject to a modified policy with an extended free cancellation window of 21 days from the date the group booking is confirmed (compared to 14 days for individuals and smaller groups).

Cancellation of the entire group booking within the 21-day window: full refund for all passengers, no fee. After the 21-day window, the standard tiered fee schedule applies to the group booking, calculated on the total group fare.

**Partial cancellations** — where some passengers in a group cancel while others continue — are assessed individually. Each departing passenger's refund is calculated based on when their individual cancellation is submitted relative to the departure date, using the standard tiered fee schedule. The group benefits of the remaining passengers are not affected unless the cancellation reduces the group below the eight-passenger threshold.

The extended 21-day window is a property of the group booking, not of individual passengers within it. A single passenger from a group of 10 cannot invoke the group's extended window as a personal benefit to cancel without fees once the 21-day period has passed.

Groups that drop below the 10-passenger threshold after booking lose the 5 percent group discount on future cancellation calculations — however, the discount already applied to the original fare is not clawed back from passengers who proceed with travel.

All group booking changes, including partial or full cancellations, must go through the Pelorus Voyages group reservations desk, not through standard bookings support.

## 3. Launch Scrub Policy

A launch scrub occurs when Pelorus Voyages postpones or cancels a departure after passengers have completed check-in at the Earth launch terminal. Scrubs are declared by the vessel captain or Pelorus Voyages mission control and may result from vessel technical issues, adverse space weather, regulatory holds, or conditions at a destination stop that make safe transit impractical.

When a scrub is declared, passengers have two options:

**Option 1 — Full refund.** All amounts paid are refunded, including any non-refundable deposits. No cancellation fee applies regardless of when the scrub is called. Refund processing follows the standard timeline for the passenger's payment method (see Section 6).

g any non-refundable deposits. No cancellation fee applies regardless of when the scrub is called. Refund processing follows the standard timeline for the passenger's payment method (see Section 6).

**Option 2 — 110 percent voyage credit.** A voyage credit equal to 110 percent of the total amount paid is applied to the passenger's Pelorus Voyages account. The additional 10 percent is Pelorus Voyages's acknowledgment of the inconvenience of a scrub. The credit is valid for 24 months from the scrub date and can be applied to any future Pelorus Voyages voyage. It cannot be converted to Orbital Points, Orbital Credits, or cash.

Passengers must elect their preferred option within 14 days of receiving the scrub notification. If no election is made within 14 days, a full refund is processed automatically.

**Orbital Points and scrubs** — Points earned on the scrubbed voyage are held in the loyalty account for 90 days from the scrub date. If the passenger rebooks within that 90-day period, the held Points are transferred to the new booking. After 90 days without a rebooking, the Points are released to the general Orbital Points balance and remain usable as standard loyalty currency.

A scrub affects a single departure date; Pelorus Voyages will reschedule the scrubbed voyage for the next available alignment window. A full cancellation of an itinerary (where Pelorus Voyages permanently discontinues the voyage) is a different situation and is communicated directly to affected passengers with separate compensation terms.

## 4. Rebooking After a Scrub

Passengers who choose the voyage credit option following a scrub may rebook on any available future departure on the same or a different itinerary. Passengers who take the refund have no special rebooking relationship with Pelorus Voyages and book afresh at current pricing.

**Credit validity and application** — voyage credits issued after a scrub are valid for 24 months from the scrub date. They can be applied to any Pelorus Voyages voyage of equal or higher value. If the new booking is more expensive than the credit, the passenger pays the difference using any accepted payment method. If the new booking is less expensive, the unused credit remainder is retained in the account for the remainder of the 24-month validity. Voyage credits do not accrue interest.

cepted payment method. If the new booking is less expensive, the unused credit remainder is retained in the account for the remainder of the 24-month validity. Voyage credits do not accrue interest.

**Priority rebooking window** — for 14 days after the scrub notification, scrub passengers have priority booking access to any future departure with remaining capacity. This allows scrub passengers to secure berths before the general booking public. After the 14-day priority window closes, rebooking proceeds at standard availability.

Passengers with scrubbed group bookings should contact the group reservations desk during the 14-day priority window to coordinate group rebooking. The group benefits associated with the original booking — priority berth access, group dining table, private briefing — are re-established on the rebooked voyage provided the group size still qualifies.

## 8. Standard Travel Insurance — Exclusions

The following are not covered by standard Pelorus Voyages travel insurance:

**Voluntary missed departures.** Any situation in which the passenger was physically capable of returning to the vessel by the muster deadline but did not do so. This includes excursion overruns, personal decisions to extend a surface stay, failure to monitor time, and equipment delays within the passenger's control.

**Solar weather scrubs.** Scrubs caused by solar particle events, coronal mass ejection warnings, or other space weather phenomena are classified as acts of nature and excluded from standard policy. Passengers can add the Extended Scrub Rider to cover solar weather events.

**Undeclared pre-existing conditions.** A condition is pre-existing if the passenger received a diagnosis, treatment, or medical advice related to it in the 12 months before the insurance purchase date. Conditions declared at purchase and cleared by a physician are covered.

Pelorus Voyages uses a three-stage payment schedule for all itinerary bookings. The deposit structure is designed to allow passengers to secure their berth early while spreading the full voyage cost closer to departure.

# Departure Planning and Scheduling Guide

This guide explains how Pelorus Voyages departure schedules work, what you need to do to meet muster deadlines at each stop, what happens if you miss a departure, and what the Outer Space Transport Compact means for passengers in an emergency. Understanding these rules before you travel is not optional — the vessel will not wait, and the costs of a missed departure are substantial.

## 1. Why Departures Cannot Wait

Pelorus Voyages departure schedules are determined by orbital mechanics, not policy. Each leg of an expedition operates within a planetary transfer window — a period when the relative positions of two bodies allow an efficient trajectory between them.

y orbital mechanics, not policy. Each leg of an expedition operates within a planetary transfer window — a period when the relative positions of two bodies allow an efficient trajectory between them. Outside that window, a transfer either requires substantially more fuel, takes significantly longer, or is not practically achievable within the voyage's fuel budget.

The Earth-Mars synodic period is approximately 26 months — that is how often Earth and Mars reach the right relative position for an efficient transfer. Pelorus Voyages schedules Inner Planets Survey and Grand Solar Tour departures during favourable alignment periods within those windows, but these are not arbitrary calendar dates. Missing the Mars departure from Moon Base 7 does not mean catching the next ship in a few days. The next scheduled Pelorus Voyages departure from Mars Colony 1 may be weeks or months away, depending on where you are in the alignment cycle.

7 does not mean catching the next ship in a few days. The next scheduled Pelorus Voyages departure from Mars Colony 1 may be weeks or months away, depending on where you are in the alignment cycle.

Within a multi-stop itinerary, each leg depends on the one before it. A two-hour hold at the Mars departure ripples forward: the Venus transfer window narrows, the Ceres approach timing shifts, and the Saturn ring transit — which requires the vessel to be positioned precisely relative to the ring plane — may be missed entirely. The schedule is not padded; every connection is load-bearing.

Departure windows at each stop are 4 to 8 hours wide. The exact window is published in the voyage manifest issued at Earth departure. Passengers should treat the muster deadline as the **latest possible moment** to board, not a target time.

No exceptions are made for late passengers, for any reason. This policy protects the 200 or more other passengers whose itinerary depends on the same departure window. If you miss departure, contact the Pelorus Voyages expedition coordinator at the stop immediately. Coordinator posts remain staffed for four hours after each departure.

**Titan is the most commonly misunderstood deadline.** Passengers frequently plan to arrive at Excursion Base Alpha 75 minutes before departure — which is the posted muster deadline — not accounting for the mandatory 20-minute cold-suit decontamination. The effective minimum return time from any Titan surface excursion is **95 minutes before the departure window**, not 75.

## 3. Missed Departure — Your Options

If you are not present at the muster point by the published deadline, the manifest closes and the vessel departs without you. Contact the Pelorus Voyages expedition coordinator station at the stop immediately. Coordinator posts remain staffed for four hours after departure.

### Voluntary vs. involuntary classification

The first thing the coordinator will determine is whether the missed departure is voluntary or involuntary. This classification directly affects what your travel insurance covers.

**Involuntary:** caused by a documented medical emergency — the passenger was physically unable to return to the vessel due to a medical event, assessed and recorded by Pelorus Voyages medical staff or a licensed physician at the stop.

**Voluntary:** everything else — excursion overruns, losing track of time, equipment delays within your control, or any personal decision to extend a surface stay. Standard travel insurance does **not** cover voluntary missed departures. The Extraction Coverage add-on is the only insurance product that covers voluntary missed departure costs.

## 4. Mining Transport and the OSTC 2038

The Outer Space Transport Compact of 2038 (OSTC) requires any commercial vessel operating in cislunar space or beyond to accept a documented distressed traveller on request, provided the vessel has life support capacity to accommodate an additional person. Mining transport operators at Moon Base 7, Ceres Waystation, and outer system waypoints are bound by this compact.

What the OSTC provides is **passage, not service.** Mining transports are working cargo vessels. The berth available to a distressed passenger is a fold-down bunk in a shared crew cabin, access to the crew galley (standard rations, no dietary options), and use of crew lavatory facilities. There is no passenger lounge, entertainment system, or medical bay beyond basic first aid.

bin, access to the crew galley (standard rations, no dietary options), and use of crew lavatory facilities. There is no passenger lounge, entertainment system, or medical bay beyond basic first aid.

The more significant limitation is **routing.** A mining transport's schedule is set by its cargo manifest. A Ceres-based transport heading toward the inner system might route through the Vesta processing station, complete two or three cargo transfers, and reach cislunar space six to eight weeks after departure. The drop-off point will be a cislunar transfer station — not Earth surface. Passengers still need to arrange their own descent from the transfer station, which adds additional cost and time.

Under the OSTC, the mining operator cannot charge the distressed traveller for passage. However, this does not make the experience free in any practical sense: weeks of additional travel time, cost of return from the transfer station, meals and personal necessities beyond crew rations, and

ever, this does not make the experience free in any practical sense: weeks of additional travel time, cost of return from the transfer station, meals and personal necessities beyond crew rations, and any other incidental costs are entirely at the passenger's expense.

Pelorus Voyages strongly recommends purchasing the **Extraction Coverage add-on** before departure. In almost every scenario, the add-on results in a faster return under substantially better conditions than a mining transport. The mining transport option is legal recourse under the OSTC and represents a genuine fallback; it should be considered a last resort, not a plan.

The Leap is an optional tether-detachment experience offered exclusively at the Ceres Waystation jump platform. It is not part of the standard surface walk and must be booked separately through the Pelorus Voyages excursion portal. At Ceres's 0.03g surface gravity, a passenger who detaches their tether and pushes off the jump platform travels upward for approximately 45 to 55 seconds before reaching an apex of roughly 80 to 100 metres, then drifts back down over the same period. Occator Crater is the most visually distinctive feature on Ceres and one of the most photographed geological sites in the asteroid belt. The crater is approximately 92 kilometres in diameter and 4 kilometres deep, with a central mound — the faculae — covered in a bright, reflective material that is clearly visible even from Earth through a telescope. The bright spots that puzzled astronomers for decades before the Dawn spacecraft provided close imaging in 2015 are composed primarily of sodium carbonate: salts deposited by briny water that percolated up from a subsurface reservoir through fractures in the crater floor and evaporated in the near-vacuum of the Cerean surface, leaving their mineral content behind.

The material from Enceladus's geysers feeds Saturn's E ring; the moon is literally building part of the ring system.

The Enceladus Geyser Flyover is a close approach to the southern plume field. The vessel passes at an altitude of approximately 25 kilometres above the surface — close enough to observe individual geyser vents and to pass through the outer fringe of the plume material. The plume is not dangerous; the material is fine ice particles and water vapour at very low density. However, it does coat the observation windows.

## 1. Ceres Waystation Overview

Ceres is the largest body in the main asteroid belt and the only dwarf planet in the inner solar system. It is approximately 940 kilometres in diameter. The Ceres Waystation is a permanent commercial and scientific installation operated by the Asteroid Belt Authority; Pelorus Voyages is one of several expedition operators with licensed access.

The Waystation Hub is a pressurised facility with a commercial concourse, a restaurant serving local and transported food, a communications relay centre, and a small exhibition on asteroid belt geology and the history of Ceres exploration. The exhibition includes the original Dawn spacecraft mission results and the subsequent discoveries about Ceres's subsurface ocean and the Occator bright deposits. It takes approximately 45 minutes to walk through and is freely accessible to all Pelorus Voyages passengers.

The Waystation's position as the outer system's main resupply and emergency hub means it has capabilities beyond its apparent size: a full medical facility, emergency docking infrastructure, and the best communications relay of any stop on the ORT or GST itinerary.

Ceres's distance from the Sun (approximately 2.7 to 3.0 AU depending on orbital position) means sunlight is significantly weaker than at Earth. The surface is dark and cold. Jupiter is distinctly non-stellar to the naked eye from the surface; Saturn is a bright point. The Milky Way at this distance from the Sun is visible with a clarity not achievable from the inner solar system.

The Surface Walk is the central experience of the Waystation stop. At 0.03g — approximately one-thirtieth of Earth's surface gravity — movement is unlike anything at any other stop on the itinerary. **Tether protocol** — all passengers are connected to a guide tether line anchored to fixed anchor points along the walking route during the standard surface walk. The tether allows full freedom of movement across the walking surface but prevents drifting beyond approximately 15 metres. A single deliberate push off the surface — both feet planted, pushing straight up — carries a passenger to roughly 15 metres before the tether draws taut. The return descent takes 20 to 30 seconds. Guides encourage at least one full arc during the familiarisation segment; it is the defining kinesthetic experience of the Ceres stop.

At 0.03g, a passenger who detaches their tether at the jump platform and pushes off travels upward for approximately 45 to 55 seconds before reaching an apex of 80 to 100 metres. They then drift back down over the same period. The full detached arc lasts approximately 90 to 110 seconds before the guide retrieves the passenger using the pole catch system at the platform base. The entire experience from platform mount to ground return is approximately five minutes.

## 5. Occator Crater Rim Tour

Occator Crater is the most visually distinctive feature on Ceres. Approximately 92 kilometres in diameter and 4 kilometres deep, its central mound is covered in bright, reflective sodium carbonate deposits — salts left behind by briny water that percolated from a subsurface reservoir through crater-floor fractures and then evaporated in the near-vacuum, leaving the mineral content behind.

The bright spots were visible from Earth-based telescopes and puzzled astronomers for decades before the Dawn spacecraft provided close imaging in 2015.

The Occator Crater Rim Tour is available as part of the standard surface excursion package for Navigator and Pathfinder passengers, or as an add-on for Pioneer passengers. The tour is conducted on the exterior rim, which provides an elevated view down into the crater floor and a clear line of sight to the main deposit complex.

## 1. Mars Colony 1 Overview

Mars Colony 1 was established in 2041 and is built into the basaltic rock of Hellas Planitia's northern shelf — a location chosen for its natural radiation shielding and proximity to confirmed subsurface water ice deposits. The colony supports approximately 2,400 permanent residents and researchers, and receives expedition visitors on a scheduled rotation coordinated with Pelorus Voyages and two other licensed operators.

The colony is a pressurised habitat complex connected by enclosed tunnels. Casual clothing is appropriate inside; no suit or helmet is required in any part of the interior. The expedition wing — where Pelorus Voyages passengers are accommodated — is maintained separately from the residential and research quarters used by permanent colonists.

Mars Colony 1 is the most terrestrially normal of the outer system stops. Gravity is 0.38g — low enough to feel light and bouncy, but high enough that movement is intuitive. Most passengers find Mars easier to adapt to than the Moon; the higher gravity reduces the vestibular disorientation some experience in very low gravity, and the three-night stay allows genuine rest and acclimatisation rather than the rapid turnaround of shorter stops.

## 2. Arriving and Living at MC-1

The transition from transit gravity (0.15g) to Martian surface gravity (0.38g) is noticeable but not dramatic — objects feel approximately twice as heavy as during transit. The first few hours in 0.38g are typically described as energising; the body has been compensating for lower gravity, and the slightly higher pull feels positive. By the end of the first day, some passengers experience mild fatigue as the body readjusts its cardiovascular baseline.

Mars Colony 1 operates on a **24-hour-40-minute Martian sol** (day). Pelorus Voyages excursion scheduling uses Earth UTC as the reference clock, but frames activity timing around the local sol to take advantage of surface light conditions. Sol 1 of the Mars stay is typically an arrival and orientation day; excursions begin on Sol 2.

## 3. Tranquility Base Heritage Site

Tranquility Base is the landing zone of Apollo 11, the first crewed lunar landing on 20 July 1969. It is protected under the Outer Space Heritage Preservation Act of 2041 and is under joint custodianship of the Lunar Heritage Authority and the Smithsonian Institution. Pelorus Voyages is a licensed excursion operator at the perimeter; passengers are brought by pressurised rover to the marked exclusion boundary and view the site from there.

From the perimeter, the following are visible: the descent stage of the Eagle lunar module, the American flag planted by the astronauts in 1969, several scientific instruments left by the crew, and the field of astronaut footprints preserved undisturbed in the regolith. Because the Moon has no atmosphere and no erosion, these features are identical to how they appeared on the day of landing.

nd the field of astronaut footprints preserved undisturbed in the regolith. Because the Moon has no atmosphere and no erosion, these features are identical to how they appeared on the day of landing. The guide will position the rover for optimal angles and can recommend viewing times based on the current sun angle.

**Heritage rules at Tranquility Base** — these are enforced under the OSHPA 2041 and violations are reported immediately to the Lunar Heritage Authority:

- No approach within the exclusion boundary under any circumstances
- No collection of surface material within the heritage zone, including material found outside the exclusion boundary
- No flash photography within 50 metres of the perimeter flagging
- No drones or remotely piloted aircraft within the heritage zone (extends 2 kilometres beyond the visible perimeter)
- No laser devices directed at the flag, descent stage, or any heritage object

## 4. Lunar Golf Links at Fra Mauro

The Lunar Golf Links is a three-hole course laid across the Fra Mauro highland basin, near the Apollo 14 landing site. Alan Shepard hit the first golf shots on the Moon here in February 1971 — one-handed, in the rigid A7L suit, with a makeshift club head attached to a contingency sample scoop. The Shepard Shot Marker, flagging the locations of Shepard's original impacts, sits approximately 400 metres south of the first tee.

Playing conditions are unlike any Earth course. The Moon's surface gravity is approximately 0.17g — one-sixth of Earth's — which means a well-struck drive travels roughly 1.2 kilometres. The first hole plays 800 metres to the green. The ball follows a long, slow arc with no atmospheric drag and no wind, and reading the lie in the regolith is the primary skill. Compacted dust behaves differently from loose granular material, and the guide will walk passengers through both.

ospheric drag and no wind, and reading the lie in the regolith is the primary skill. Compacted dust behaves differently from loose granular material, and the guide will walk passengers through both.

All rounds are played in articulated ClearSuit Pro suits, which allow a full two-handed swing — a significant improvement over Shepard's one-handed attempt. Equipment is provided: six clubs and two balls per player are included in the excursion price. Personal clubs may be brought from Earth but count against the passenger's personal mass allowance. Any personal clubs must be presented to the Moon Base 7 equipment desk at least 2 hours before the excursion for pressurisation assessment.

**Three stops along the route:**

The first stop is the Apennine Foothills overlook — an elevated ridge with a 360-degree view of the surrounding mare. The guide explains the geology of the impact basins and the origin of the mare's relatively smooth surface compared to the heavily cratered highlands.

## 1. The Outer System in Context

Saturn is approximately 1.2 to 1.5 billion kilometres from Earth depending on orbital position. At that distance, one-way light travel time is 43 to 84 minutes; a question sent to Earth receives a reply 86 to 168 minutes later. Real-time conversation is not feasible. The Milky Way is visible from the outer system with a clarity impossible from the inner solar system — the reduced solar glare reveals structure in the night sky that is simply washed out at Earth's distance.

The Ceres-to-Saturn transit takes approximately five days. This is the longest single transit leg on any itinerary. The vessel's programming schedule for this leg typically includes the full complement of science officer lectures; the outer system approaches to Saturn, Titan, and Enceladus are subjects the science

The vessel's programming schedule for this leg typically includes the full complement of science officer lectures; the outer system approaches to Saturn, Titan, and Enceladus are subjects the science officer covers in depth on the inbound leg so that passengers arrive at each stop with context.

The outer system stop sequence after Ceres is: Saturn Ring Transit (6 hours, no disembarkation) → Titan Ice Flats (surface excursion) → Enceladus Geyser Flyover (passive observation) → return transit to Earth (8 to 9 days). The total time from Ceres departure to Earth return is approximately 14 to 15 days.

## 2. Saturn Ring Transit

The Saturn Ring Transit is a six-hour passage between the B and C rings of Saturn's ring system. There is no docking, no EVA, and no disembarkation. The vessel moves slowly through the ring plane while passengers observe from the observation deck.

ween the B and C rings of Saturn's ring system. There is no docking, no EVA, and no disembarkation. The vessel moves slowly through the ring plane while passengers observe from the observation deck.

**What the rings actually are** — the ring system at the B-C boundary is not the solid sheet it appears to be from Earth. It is composed of ice and rock particles ranging from dust grains to objects the size of houses, distributed across a band roughly 270,000 kilometres in diameter but only about 10 metres to a kilometre thick. The vessel passes through the Cassini Division boundary area, where particle density is low enough to be safe. The primary hazard is microparticle impact on the outer hull — expected, accounted for in maintenance schedules, not dangerous to passengers.

**The visual experience** depends on the sun angle at the time of transit, which varies with Saturn's position in its 29-year orbit and the vessel's approach geometry.

## 3. Titan Ice Flats

Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the only moon in the solar system with a dense atmosphere — a thick nitrogen layer with a surface pressure roughly 1.5 times Earth's. The surface is a landscape of hydrocarbon lakes, methane rivers, and plains of water-ice overlaid with organic sediment. At minus 179 degrees Celsius, it is among the coldest surfaces on which any Pelorus Voyages passenger will set foot.

The Titan Ice Flats excursion takes place on the frozen shoreline of Kraken Mare, the largest of Titan's methane seas. The water-ice surface here is compacted enough to support surface sports.

Combined with the dense nitrogen atmosphere (which provides aerodynamic effects even at lower speeds), movement on the surface feels heavier than Ceres but still dramatically lighter than Mars or Earth. ## 4. Enceladus Geyser Flyover

Enceladus is the final destination before the return transit to Earth. It is a small icy moon — only 500 kilometres in diameter — with a global ocean of liquid water beneath its ice shell. Active geysers at the southern polar region continuously vent material from this subsurface ocean into space: water vapour, ice particles, and organic compounds that feed Saturn's E ring. Enceladus is literally constructing part of the ring system in real time.

**The encounter** — the vessel makes a close approach at approximately 25 kilometres altitude above the southern plume field. At this altitude, individual geyser vents are visible and the outer fringe of the plume material is directly encountered.

roach at approximately 25 kilometres altitude above the southern plume field. At this altitude, individual geyser vents are visible and the outer fringe of the plume material is directly encountered. The plume is composed of fine ice particles and water vapour at very low density — not dangerous, but it coats the observation windows. Cleaning requires approximately four hours and is factored into the schedule; observation window visibility may be reduced for the last hour of the approach and the beginning of the post-encounter transit.

**Why there is no EVA and no surface access** — planetary protection protocols prohibit any contact between Earth-origin materials and the Enceladus surface or plume zone below a minimum altitude threshold. The 25-kilometre approach altitude is set by these protocols, not by operational preference.

between Earth-origin materials and the Enceladus surface or plume zone below a minimum altitude threshold. The 25-kilometre approach altitude is set by these protocols, not by operational preference. Enceladus is one of the strongest candidate locations for extraterrestrial life in the solar system; the protocols exist to prevent Earth-origin contamination from confounding future life-detection measurements. The vessel's science officer explains the protocols and the astrobiological case for Enceladus in the dedicated pre-flyover lecture.

**The observation** — the encounter is entirely from the observation deck and the vessel's observation windows. The science officer provides a narrated briefing covering:
- The evidence for subsurface liquid water

## 1. The Aphrodite — Overview and Environment

The Aphrodite is positioned at 52 kilometres altitude in the Venusian upper cloud deck. At this altitude, the temperature outside the station is approximately 75 degrees Celsius, the pressure is similar to Earth at surface, and the surrounding atmosphere is composed of carbon dioxide with sulphuric acid cloud droplets. The station is sealed and pressurised; passengers experience none of this directly. Inside, the atmosphere is Earth-normal and the gravity is 0.88g — the closest to Earth of any destination on any Pelorus Voyages itinerary.

**The gravity transition** is the first thing most passengers notice. After days in the 0.15g transit environment and on Mars at 0.38g, 0.88g feels unexpectedly heavy. Arms feel heavier, movement takes more effort, and some passengers experience mild fatigue in the first 24 hours.

n the 0.15g transit environment and on Mars at 0.38g, 0.88g feels unexpectedly heavy. Arms feel heavier, movement takes more effort, and some passengers experience mild fatigue in the first 24 hours. This is normal and does not require medical attention unless accompanied by cardiac symptoms. Pelorus Voyages provides a wellness orientation on arrival with stretching guidance, hydration recommendations, and a pacing suggestion for the first day. The 24 hours after Venus arrival is not the time to push physical activity.

**The station's motion** — The Aphrodite does not anchor to a fixed position. It drifts with the Venusian superrotating winds, which travel at approximately 300 kilometres per hour at cloud deck altitude and complete a full circuit of the planet every four Earth days. The Glass Floor Tour is a 90-minute guided experience along the underside observation corridor of The Aphrodite. A pressurised walkway runs the full length of the station's lower hull. The floor is made of 4-centimetre borosilicate glass panels, rated to withstand the pressure differential and the mechanical loads of the drifting station. Below the glass: 52 kilometres of Venusian atmosphere, the upper cloud layer churning in gold and amber below, and far below that the faint orange glow of the surface.

The guide narrates throughout — cloud chemistry, the lightning patterns visible in the lower deck, what the surface conditions actually are at 465 degrees Celsius and 90 Earth atmospheres — and stops at four viewing stations where the glass sections are widest

g patterns visible in the lower deck, what the surface conditions actually are at 465 degrees Celsius and 90 Earth atmospheres — and stops at four viewing stations where the glass sections are widest for clearest viewing.

Most passengers stop walking about halfway through. The visual disconnect between standing normally in a well-lit pressurised corridor and looking directly down into a planetary atmosphere is not something photographs prepare visitors for. A few passengers lie flat on the glass to eliminate the peripheral frame of the corridor walls. The guide adjusts the pace to whatever the group needs.

## 4. The Gondola Descent

The Gondola Descent is The Aphrodite's most exclusive experience and requires the most advance planning. It involves boarding a pressurised observation pod — the gondola — that detaches from the station's lower hull and descends approximately 3 kilometres into the Venusian upper cloud layer. The descent takes about 15 minutes. Passengers spend roughly 45 minutes inside the cloud layer before the gondola ascends and redocks with the station. Total duration from boarding to exit is approximately 90 minutes.

Inside the cloud layer, the sulphuric acid aerosol creates haze ranging from translucent to near-opaque. The gondola windows fog and clear in cycles as the pod moves through regions of varying cloud density.

he cloud layer, the sulphuric acid aerosol creates haze ranging from translucent to near-opaque. The gondola windows fog and clear in cycles as the pod moves through regions of varying cloud density. Outside temperature during the descent reaches approximately 75 degrees Celsius, visible as a slight shimmer on the panel seals. Inside the gondola, the temperature is standard cabin temperature. The experience is quiet, slightly disorienting, and unlike anything else on any Pelorus Voyages itinerary.

## 5. Venus Science Centre

The Aphrodite Science Centre occupies Deck 4 of the station and is dedicated to the defining scientific question of the modern era of Venus exploration: is there life in the clouds of Venus? The centre is open to all cabin classes at no additional charge and takes approximately one to two hours to walk through at a comfortable pace.

**The phosphine detection** is the centrepiece exhibit. In 2020, a team of astronomers reported detection of phosphine — a gas associated with biological processes on Earth — in the Venusian atmosphere at concentrations that could not easily be explained by known abiotic chemistry.

ers reported detection of phosphine — a gas associated with biological processes on Earth — in the Venusian atmosphere at concentrations that could not easily be explained by known abiotic chemistry. The detection was significant because the cloud deck altitude where phosphine was detected (50 to 60 kilometres, overlapping with The Aphrodite's position) is, in terms of temperature and pressure, among the most Earth-like environments in the solar system outside Earth itself. Subsequent analyses have been mixed — some confirming a spectral feature consistent with phosphine at lower concentrations, others finding the original signal difficult to reproduce. The debate is ongoing in the published literature.

**The atmospheric life hypothesis** — the second major exhibit traces what would need to be true for life to exist in the Venusian atmosphere. The cloud droplets are sulphuric acid, which is hostile to life as understood on Earth.

The hypothesis involves hypothetical microorganisms suspended in the atmosphere that have adapted to manage the acid environment — not living in the clouds but using them as habitat. The exhibit explains why this is less implausible than it sounds and what biochemical preconditions such adaptation would require. It also clearly explains what the hypothesis cannot account for, and why the mainstream scientific position remains sceptical.

**The working research station** — a collaboration between the Pelorus Voyages Science Programme and two university partners operates on Deck 4. Samples of the plume material that coats the observation windows are periodically analysed here.

Visitors can observe the analysis process through a glass partition and speak with researchers during scheduled public hours. The research station produces ongoing data incorporated into the centre's exhibits in near-real-time — it is one of the few functioning research operations accessible to civilian visitors anywhere in the solar system.

Mars Colony 1 is the primary human settlement on Mars and the anchor of the Inner Planets Survey and Grand Solar Tour Mars stay. Established in 2041, MC-1 is a pressurised habitat complex built into the basaltic rock of Hellas Planitia's northern shelf, chosen for its natural radiation shielding and proximity to subsurface water ice deposits. The colony supports a permanent population of approximately 2,400 residents and receives expedition visitors on a scheduled rotation coordinated with Pelorus Voyages and two other licensed operators.

Passengers spend three nights at MC-1. The accommodation is in the expedition wing, which is maintained separately from the residential quarters used by colony permanent residents and researchers. Expedition wing rooms are private for Navigator and Pathfinder class passengers and shared for Pioneer class passengers; shared rooms accommodate two passengers of the same gender assignment.

The Cydonia Highlands formation complex is located in the northern lowlands of Mars, approximately 600 kilometres north-northwest of Mars Colony 1. The formations at Cydonia are a collection of mesa-like structures with distinctive geometry — in particular a roughly 3-kilometre-wide formation that, when photographed by the Viking 1 orbiter in 1976, appeared to bear a resemblance to a humanoid face due to lighting and image compression artefacts. The "Face on Mars" generated decades of popular speculation and became one of the most-discussed features in the history of planetary exploration.

Hellas Planitia is the largest impact basin on Mars and one of the largest confirmed impact structures in the solar system, spanning approximately 2,300 kilometres in diameter and reaching 7.2 kilometres below the Martian mean surface level — making its floor the lowest point on Mars and one of the lowest surfaces on any rocky planet. The Hellas Basin Overlook excursion is a half-day trip from Mars Colony 1 to a vantage point on the basin's northwestern rim, providing a view into the depression and across the extraordinary scale of the landscape.

The practical experience of the overlook is unlike standing at the edge of a canyon. Hellas is too large for its depth to be immediately apparent; the human eye cannot take in a structure 2,300 kilometres across from a single viewpoint. What is apparent is the atmospheric difference.

Hellas is too large for its depth to be immediately apparent; the human eye cannot take in a structure 2,300 kilometres across from a single viewpoint. What is apparent is the atmospheric difference. The floor of Hellas sits deep enough below the mean surface level that atmospheric pressure there is measurably higher than at MC-1 — approximately 20 to 30 percent higher at the lowest points, which is still far below breathable levels but high enough to affect dust dynamics and occasionally support short-lived liquid water films in the lowest sections. On clear days, the haze at the basin floor is visible as a distinct layer, a ghost of a thicker atmosphere that exists nowhere else on Mars.

The Hellas Basin Overlook is best experienced at sunrise. The Martian dawn at the rim location catches the basin in a particular light that is almost impossible to photograph faithfully — the shadow line moving across the basin floor is a slow, vast shift of light that takes more than an hour to

Pelorus Voyages schedules the Hellas excursion as a sunrise excursion whenever possible; the departure from MC-1 is before local sunrise on those days, typically around 0430 MC-1 time.

No EVA is required at the overlook itself; the viewing area is accessible via pressurised transport rover with an open viewing section under a filtered dome. Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in the solar system. It rises approximately 21.9 kilometres above the Martian mean surface level and spans roughly 600 kilometres at its base — larger than the state of Arizona. The shield volcano has been volcanically inactive for tens of millions of years but remains intact due to Mars's lack of plate tectonics, which on Earth cause volcanic structures to erode and subduct over geological time. The caldera at the summit is 80 kilometres in diameter and contains a complex of nested pit structures formed by successive collapse events as magma chambers emptied during past eruptions.

The Caldera Rim excursion is a Pathfinder class-exclusive experience available on Inner Planets Survey and Grand Solar Tour voyages with Mars stays. It involves a pressurised shuttle flight from Mars Colony 1 to a base camp at approximately 19 kilometres elevation, a guide-led traverse to the caldera rim at 21.9 kilometres, and a return to base camp for the shuttle

urised shuttle flight from Mars Colony 1 to a base camp at approximately 19 kilometres elevation, a guide-led traverse to the caldera rim at 21.9 kilometres, and a return to base camp for the shuttle flight back. Total excursion duration is approximately 10 hours. The caldera rim presents an unobstructed view into a collapse complex 80 kilometres wide and several kilometres deep; the scale is not intuitively graspable from a single viewpoint, and most passengers describe a period of simply sitting at the rim attempting to understand what they are looking at.

The Olympus Fitness Test is a prerequisite for the Caldera Rim excursion and must be completed at Mars Colony 1 at least 48 hours before the scheduled excursion departure. The test assesses cardiovascular and musculoskeletal capacity for sustained exertion in the Mars EVA suit at Martian atmospheric pressure and gravity conditions.

The Terraforming Operations Zone is an active working site approximately 40 kilometres northwest of Mars Colony 1. Pelorus Voyages operates guided tours of the zone for Navigator and Pathfinder class passengers; Pioneer passengers may purchase the tour as an add-on. Transportation from MC-1 is by pressurised transport rover; the journey takes approximately 35 minutes each way.

The terraforming project at this site focuses on atmospheric seeding: a series of large-scale aerosol dispersal installations pump catalytic compounds into the lower Martian atmosphere to gradually thicken it and raise the surface temperature. The process is measured in decades and centuries, not years, and the effect of any single visit on the long-term atmospheric profile is effectively zero — visitors are not observing dramatic change but rather the scale and organisation of an engineering effort intended to outlast any individual human lifetime.

The Lunar Golf Links is a three-hole course laid across the Fra Mauro highland basin near the Apollo 14 landing site. It is the only sanctioned golf course on the Moon and one of the most distinctive sporting experiences in the solar system. The course operates under the management of the Fra Mauro Excursion Authority and is accessible to Pelorus Voyages passengers holding Navigator or Pathfinder cabin class, or through add-on purchase for Pioneer passengers.

Playing conditions are unlike any course on Earth. The Moon's gravity is approximately one-sixth of Earth's, which means a well-struck drive — identical swing, identical club, identical ball — will travel roughly 1.2 kilometres. The first hole plays 800 metres to the green; the approach shot on a typical par-four Earth course becomes the tee shot here. The ball follows a long, slow arc with no atmospheric drag or wind to redirect it.

Reading lies is the primary skill; the regolith has texture ranging from compacted dust to loose granular material, and ball behaviour on the surface varies accordingly.

All rounds are played in modern articulated surface suits, which allow a full two-handed swing. This is a significant improvement over Alan Shepard's 1971 one-handed shots, which he managed in the rigid A7L suit with a makeshift club head attached to a contingency sample scoop. Tranquility Base Heritage Site is the landing zone of Apollo 11, the first crewed lunar landing, which took place on 20 July 1969. The site is protected under the Outer Space Heritage Preservation Act of 2041, which established an exclusion boundary around the landing zone and placed the site under joint custodianship of the Lunar Heritage Authority and the Smithsonian Institution. Pelorus Voyages is a licensed excursion operator at the perimeter and provides guided viewing access to GST passengers with the extended Moon Base 7 layover.

Passengers are brought to the marked perimeter by pressurised rover. From the perimeter, the flag, the descent stage of the Eagle lunar module, several scientific instruments, and the astronaut footprint field are visible. The perimeter itself is the closest any visitor may approach; there is no closer access under any circumstances.

The Outer Space Heritage Preservation Act carries criminal penalties for entry within the exclusion boundary, and Pelorus Voyages guides are required to report any violation immediately.

Photography from the perimeter is encouraged and the viewing conditions are excellent. The guide will position the rover for optimal angles and can recommend times of the lunar day when the low sun angle produces the best shadowing on the descent stage and footprint field.

The Saturn Ring Transit is a six-hour passive observation experience during which the Pelorus Voyages vessel makes a slow traversal between the B and C rings of Saturn's ring system. It is available on the Outer Reaches Tour and Grand Solar Tour and is the only stop on any itinerary that involves no planetary surface, no EVA, and no disembarkation. The vessel does not dock at anything; it simply moves through the ring plane at low speed while passengers observe from the observation deck.

The ring plane at the B-C boundary is not the dense, solid sheet it appears from Earth. The rings are composed of ice and rock particles ranging in size from dust grains to objects the size of houses, distributed across a band that is roughly 270,000 kilometres in diameter but only about 10 metres to a kilometre thick at any given point.

The vessel passes through a region where the particle density is low enough to be safe — the B-C Cassini Division boundary area — and the primary hazard is microparticle impact on the outer hull, which is expected and accounted for in vessel maintenance schedules. Passengers are never in danger.

The visual experience depends heavily on the sun angle at the time of transit, which varies with Saturn's position in its 29-year orbit and the vessel's approach geometry. In favourable sun angles, the rings are starkly lit from one side: a sweeping, backlit arc of ice filling the sky. In less favourable angles, they appear as a muted band of grey-white.

Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the only moon in the solar system with a dense atmosphere. Its surface is a landscape of hydrocarbon lakes, methane rivers, and plains of water-ice overlaid with organic sediment. The Titan Ice Flats excursion takes place on the frozen shoreline of Kraken Mare, the largest of Titan's methane seas, where the water-ice surface is compacted enough to support low-gravity surface sports. The excursion is available exclusively to Outer Reaches Tour and Grand Solar Tour passengers.

Surface gravity on Titan is approximately 0.14g — slightly less than the Moon. In combination with Titan's dense nitrogen atmosphere, which provides aerodynamic effects similar to Earth at lower speeds, movement on the surface feels heavy compared to Ceres but still dramatically low compared to Earth or Mars. Jumps are high; speed is achievable with minimal effort; falling is slow and rarely results in injury with proper suit technique.

The Aphrodite is a floating resort station positioned at 52 kilometres altitude in the Venusian atmosphere, within the upper cloud deck. It is the only stop on any Pelorus Voyages itinerary where gravity closely matches Earth — the surface gravity of Venus is 0.9g, and at cloud deck altitude the effective gravity experienced on the station is approximately 0.88g. For most passengers, who will have spent the preceding days or weeks in microgravity transit and at Mars's 0.38g, arriving at The Aphrodite feels unexpectedly heavy. A brief wellness orientation is provided to all passengers on arrival, and 24 to 48 hours of mild fatigue is normal as the body readjusts. This is not a medical event and does not require a report to the vessel's medical officer unless accompanied by other symptoms.

The station drifts with the Venusian atmosphere's superrotating wind patterns, which travel at approximately 300 kilometres per hour at cloud deck altitude and complete a full circuit of the planet

The station drifts with the Venusian atmosphere's superrotating wind patterns, which travel at approximately 300 kilometres per hour at cloud deck altitude and complete a full circuit of the planet every four Earth days. The Aphrodite does not fight the wind — it is designed to drift with it. Over a standard three-night stay, the station travels roughly one-third of the way around Venus. The view from the observation decks changes continuously; no two viewing periods offer the same angle on the cloud formations below.

Two views define The Aphrodite experience and exist in striking contrast. Looking upward from the observation decks, passengers see clear sky: the sun, visibly larger and approximately 1.9 times brighter than from Earth, stars at night unobscured by atmosphere above the cloud deck.

The Aphrodite Science Centre occupies Deck 4 of the resort station and is dedicated to the question that has defined modern astrobiology: is there life in the clouds of Venus? The centre presents the available evidence without advocacy and without conclusion. Pelorus Voyages takes no position on the question, and the exhibits are designed in consultation with active researchers on both sides of the debate.

The centrepiece exhibit is the phosphine detection of 2020. A team of astronomers reported the detection of phosphine — a gas associated with biological processes on Earth — in the Venusian atmosphere at concentrations that could not be easily explained by known abiotic chemistry. The announcement was significant because the conditions at the cloud deck altitude where phosphine was detected (around 50 to 60 kilometres) are, in terms of temperature and pressure, among the most Earth-like environments in the solar system outside Earth itself.

oud deck altitude where phosphine was detected (around 50 to 60 kilometres) are, in terms of temperature and pressure, among the most Earth-like environments in the solar system outside Earth itself. The detection has since been scrutinised intensely; some follow-up analyses have confirmed a spectral feature consistent with phosphine at lower concentrations, others have found the original signal difficult to reproduce, and the debate remains unresolved in the published literature as of the most recent exhibits update.

The second major exhibit traces what would need to be true for life to exist in the Venusian atmosphere. The cloud droplets themselves are sulphuric acid — hostile to life as we understand it — but the hypothesis involves life not in the clouds but using the clouds: hypothetical microorganisms suspended in the atmosphere that have adapted to manage the acid environment.

It also explains what it would not explain, and why the hypothesis has critics.

**The summit of the solar system's largest volcano. 21.9 kilometres above the Martian surface. An 80-kilometre-wide caldera at your feet.**

Olympus Mons rises higher than any mountain on Earth and spans a base larger than the state of Arizona. It has been dormant for tens of millions of years. **The only place in the solar system where a single step sends you 100 metres into space.**

At 0.03g, Ceres has the lowest surface gravity of any Pelorus Voyages destination. The Leap takes full advantage of it. You step onto the jump platform, detach your tether, plant both feet, and push off. You travel upward for 45 to 55 seconds. You reach an apex of 80 to 100 metres above the Cerean surface. There is no sensation of falling — the vestibular system at 0.03g registers motion as drift, not drop. Participants consistently report it as floating, not jumping.

# Tranquility Base Heritage Walk — Moon Base 7

**The landing site of Apollo 11, preserved exactly as it was on 20 July 1969. The flag is still there. The footprints are still there. Nothing has changed.**

The Moon has no atmosphere, no weather, no erosion. The Eagle lunar module's descent stage, the American flag, the scientific instruments, and the field of footprints left by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin have not moved since 1969. They are identical to the day they were left. No monument on Earth is as perfectly preserved as Tranquility Base, because nothing on Earth stands still for 60 years without wind, water, and time wearing it down.

Pelorus Voyages brings Grand Solar Tour passengers to the marked exclusion boundary by pressurised rover. From there, everything is visible: the descent stage, the flag, the instruments, the footprint field.

The Pelorus Voyages fusion drive maintains a sustained 0.15g acceleration throughout each transit leg — low enough to be comfortable for most passengers and high enough to prevent the bone density and fluid shift problems associated with true microgravity. However, the departure phase from Earth and the final deceleration approach to each destination produce brief periods of higher acceleration.

The Earth departure burn lasts approximately 45 minutes and reaches a peak of 2.2g during the first eight minutes before the drive throttles down to the sustained transit level. This is the highest g-load passengers experience during the voyage. At 2.2g, passengers feel approximately twice their normal body weight. This is within the comfortable tolerance range for healthy adults; most passengers experience it as a firm pressure and a slight shortness of breath.

Passengers with significant cardiovascular conditions should discuss this peak specifically with their physician when obtaining medical clearance, not just spaceflight in general.

Arrival burns — decelerating to match the destination's orbital velocity — produce a similar but typically shorter peak. Arrival at Moon Base 7 involves a 20-minute burn at up to 1.8g. Arrival at Mars Colony 1 involves a 35-minute burn at up to 1.9g, slightly longer due to the greater distance traversed. Arrival at Venus is shorter at 1.7g peak due to the drive's higher relative efficiency in the inner solar system at that point. Arrival at Ceres involves 1.6g peak for approximately 25 minutes.

## 3. Earth to Moon Base 7 (Days 1–2)

The Earth departure burn is the most intense acceleration phase of the voyage — a 45-minute burn with a peak of 2.2g in the first 8 minutes before the drive throttles to the sustained 0.15g transit level. All passengers must be secured in their berths with acceleration harnesses during the burn. The departure burn schedule is announced 30 minutes in advance by vessel intercom.

After the burn, 0.15g transit gravity takes over. Most passengers notice it immediately — objects feel lighter, liquids need sealed containers, and the inner ear begins its adjustment. The first 48 to 72 hours involve mild adaptation symptoms for many passengers (head congestion, slight nausea, a sensation of floating while seated).

## 7. Ceres to Saturn (Days 9–13)

The 5-day Ceres-to-Saturn transit is the longest single leg on the ORT. By Day 13, one-way light delay to Earth is 43 to 84 minutes. ## 8. Saturn Ring Transit (Day 14)

Six hours drifting through the B-C ring boundary. No docking, no EVA, no disembarkation. At 100,000 kilometres above Saturn's cloud tops, the planet subtends approximately 30 degrees of sky — it is not something your eye can take in all at once. The rings in the best illumination conditions are a sweeping backlit arc; in lower-contrast conditions, a muted grey-white band. The voyage manifest specifies the expected illumination quality.

Observation deck open all 6 hours. Outer deck sealed (microparticle risk). Bar and dining room open.

**Observation deck closes 30 minutes before the ring exit burn.** Be on the deck before the close if you want the full transit.

## 9. Saturn to Titan (Days 14–15)

The 8-hour Saturn-to-Titan transit follows immediately after the Ring Transit. Titan orbits Saturn at approximately 1.2 million kilometres — a brief hop after the 5-day Ceres-Saturn leg. Titan becomes visibly larger over the transit and its thick nitrogen atmosphere is detectable as the horizon haze in approach views. The science officer typically holds an informal Q&A on the transit deck during this brief leg.

Eight hours at Titan. Surface gravity 0.14g. Surface temperature: minus 179 degrees Celsius. Cold suit mandatory and non-optional — provided by Pelorus Voyages, not rented. Ice sports available: low-gravity skating on groomed track sections, sled racing on downhill lanes, long-jump from a dedicated launch zone.

## 11. Enceladus Geyser Flyover (Days 15–16)

Twenty hours after departing Titan, the vessel makes its 25-kilometre altitude approach to Enceladus's southern plume field. The encounter lasts approximately 4 hours. No EVA, no surface access — planetary protection protocols prohibit surface contact. Passive observation from the deck and vessel windows.

The plume coats observation windows; cleaning begins approximately 4 hours after the encounter. Window visibility may be reduced for the final hour of the approach.

The Enceladus stop is typically the emotional close of the outer system sequence. Most passengers describe a period of quiet at the departure from Enceladus. The return transit begins immediately.

## 12. Enceladus to Earth Return (Days 17–24)

The return transit from Enceladus to Earth takes 8 to 9 days. The return arc does not retrace the outbound route. This is the longest uninterrupted transit of the ORT and is typically the most relaxed stretch of the voyage. The bar hosts the voyage retrospective social event during this leg.

By the first Earth morning after arrival on Day 24, Earth gravity feels genuinely heavy to most passengers. Give yourself the rest of the arrival day; most people who go directly from a 24-day voyage to full work or activity schedules on arrival day report significant fatigue.

ORT does not visit Mars or Venus. The Moon Base 7 layover is 4 hours (transit + certifications only), identical to IPS. Passengers who want Mars, Venus, or the Moon shore excursions must book the Grand Solar Tour. The ORT departs directly from the Moon toward Ceres, bypassing the inner planets.

## 3. Redeeming Orbital Points

Redemption requires a minimum of **5,000 Points per transaction**. Points are redeemed through the account portal — they cannot be applied at the excursion desk, the bar, or any other point of sale during the voyage.

**Voyage credit** — the most common redemption method. Navigate to booking checkout, select the Points redemption option, and choose how many Points to apply. The portal converts the selected Points into a voyage credit that offsets the payment due. Conversion rate: 1 point = USD 1 equivalent of voyage credit. 5,000 points = USD 50 voyage credit. Fractional redemptions above the 5,000-point minimum are permitted — you may apply exactly the number you wish.

**Cabin class upgrade** — use the Upgrade function in the account portal and select Points as the payment method. Points redemption for upgrades is available until **seven days before the departure window opens**. After that seven-day cutoff, upgrades must be paid by credit card, debit card, or Orbital Credits — Points cannot be used for upgrades within seven days of departure, regardless of loyalty tier.

**Excursion purchases** — Points can be applied when purchasing excursions through the portal before departure. Points cannot be used at the excursion desk on the day. All Points-based excursion purchases must be completed before departure from Earth.

**Pending Points cannot be redeemed** — Points earned on a voyage-in-progress or not-yet-departed voyage are pending and cannot be applied to another booking until the voyage departs.

**Points not refunded on cancellation** — Points that have been redeemed and applied to a booking are not restored if the booking is subsequently cancelled. The cancellation refund covers the cash component of the payment; the Points portion is not returned.

A medical emergency that occurs during a transit leg — between destinations, away from any facility — is handled by the vessel's medical bay as the first response. The flight surgeon assesses the situation and determines whether the condition can be managed aboard for the remainder of the leg, or whether the vessel needs to divert to the nearest appropriate facility. ## 5. Pregnancy Policy

Passengers who are pregnant at the time of departure may travel provided the pregnancy is **less than 12 weeks gestation on the departure date**. The 12-week limit is calculated from the first day of the last menstrual period as documented in the medical clearance; it is not an estimate. The clearance letter must state the gestational age explicitly and confirm it will be less than 12 weeks on the departure date.

The 12-week cutoff is absolute and cannot be waived by any physician letter, special clearance, or other mechanism. This policy exists because the vessel's medical infrastructure is not equipped to manage obstetric emergencies beyond very early pregnancy, and because the radiation environment of deep space — while managed for typical passengers — has not been established as safe

not equipped to manage obstetric emergencies beyond very early pregnancy, and because the radiation environment of deep space — while managed for typical passengers — has not been established as safe for fetal development at any gestational stage.

If an ultrasound or revised assessment moves the gestational age to 12 weeks or beyond before departure, this constitutes medical disqualification. The passenger is entitled to a full refund of all amounts paid and should not process a standard cancellation — contact bookings support to initiate the medical disqualification claim.

For passengers who become pregnant after booking: if the pregnancy will be at 12 weeks or beyond on the departure date, the booking cannot proceed. Whether the cancellation qualifies as medical disqualification or standard cancellation (with fees) depends on whether the pregnancy itself is the medically documented reason travel is impossible, versus a personal decision not to travel while pregnant.

*Anticoagulants* (warfarin/Coumadin, rivaroxaban/Xarelto, apixaban/Eliquis, dabigatran/Pradaxa) — fluid shifts in low gravity affect distribution and the g-load phases add cardiovascular stress. Discuss dosing with the prescribing physician and the Pelorus Voyages flight surgeon in advance.
